rv.q: As Bartlett tells it, with searing insight and mocking wit in a flawless production directed by Michael Mayer, this was the generation that grabbed everything with both hands — and then ate their young.

"'What did you stand for? Nothing except being able to do whatever the f!!k you wanted.' Harsh, yes, and let’s admit somewhat broad for a generation that included at least a few societal game changers. Yet still ringing of truth, especially in the performances that Mayer has drawn from this amazing quintet...
It's a testament to Bartlett's clever, incisive dialogue that such selfish, limited people should steal our hearts.
And yet I have to admit I had a swell time at 'Love, Love, Love,' a Roundabout Theater Company production, impeccably directed by Michael Mayer and featuring a nigh-perfect five-member ensemble.
While Love, Love, Love is not quite as profound as it intends to be, there's an awfully lot in it to, well, love.
Putting broader meanings aside, the two-hour drama is a spectacular showcase for marvelous actors to age and transform into almost unrecognizable versions of the same characters.
The problem is not only that these sweeping condemnations are overfamiliar and overbroad but that the play in no way supports them.
"Love, Love, Love" left me both amused, and consumed by thoughts about fortune and fate.
No one is particularly likable in this play, and that is very much the source of its hilarity.
The first two acts initially seem short and slight, but the play as a whole pays off in the end.
Michael Mayer's direction is fluid and the acting is sublime, but it's hard to love, love, love the fact that Bartlett spells things out so baldly.

“British actor Richard Armitage making his New York stage debut and Tony and Academy Award nominee Amy Ryan work hard to make Kenneth and Sandra three-dimensional, likeable people, but, as written by Mr. Bartlett, their crassness is the fatal flaw in ‘Love, Love, Love’.

Love, Love, Love might have redeemed itself if it contained a modicum of the love its title boasts, or if any of these characters had even the slightest bit of an arc, but — spoiler alert? — they don't.
This play needs to be seen, produced and shown to a public that needs to laugh, needs to think and needs to be shown the truth.
The comedy is superbly portrayed by this well-chosen cast—Armitage and Ryan the perfect yin and yang, ever so delicately brought to life by Michael Mayer's fine directorial hand.
Bartlett (Cock, King Charles III) is a great writer and a keen observer of relationships, and he proves as much with this decade-spanning serio-comedy.
These bitter questions about life come sugarcoated in a smart and fast-moving comedy, which makes them easy to swallow and take some time to digest after the show.

"Guideposts from the Baby Boomers, the Me Generation, and the Millennials emerge shining with palpable irony and, under Mayer's direction, five razor-sharp cast members portray characters who are well-carved, poked at and picked apart for detailed authenticity...
Mr. Armitage finds Ken's inner child and nurtures him into a charming, successful business man who is also a complete failure.

"The five actors, whom Michael Mayer directs with utmost authority, play together well. Needing to present characters who age 44 years, Ryan and Armitage have the biggest challenges, and they come out okay, if best suited to Act II. Rosenfield’s Jamie and Kazan’s Rose only age 21 years and come out OK, too.
It's kind of a bummer, even if there is truth in playwright Mike Bartlett's storytelling.
I was enthralled by 'Love, Love, Love.' The cast was stellar.
This ensemble cast is superb... Sets, divine...Michael Mayer must have had so much fun directing this one.

cn.t: Bartlett's scathing generational satire earns mostly positive reviews for its biting wit and stellar performances by Ryan and Armitage, though some critics find its portrait of selfish boomers too harsh and one-note.
